newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Greenpeace returns nuclear waste to Belgian owner.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace returns nuclear waste to Belgian owner.

text.p: Greenpeace said on Wednesday it gave nuclear waste piped into the sea by a French re-processing plant back to its rightful owner -- a Belgian power plant.

The environmental group said management of the Doel plant had accepted samples of the waste for safe-keeping, but the company which operates the plant near the port of Antwerp said Greenpeace misrepresented the radio-activity of the waste.

Greenpeace collected the samples -- 250 grammes of sediment and 150 milli-litres of water -- from the Channel near the La Hague plant in Cherbourg, France, which reprocesses spent nuclear fuel from countries including Germany and Belgium.
It said in a statement that the Belgian government had insisted Electrabel, the Belgian company which operates the Doel plant, take the waste back.

"In accepting what came from them by rights Electrabel is showing first signs of good will. It is now urgent that it decides to stop dumping its radio-active waste in the sea immediately," Greenpeace Belgium spokesman Jan Vande Putte said.
By sending spent fuel to La Hague, Belgian nuclear plants were also responsible for the contamination of the marine environment, he said.

Greenpeace warned that in the next three years 669 tonnes of highly radio-active nuclear fuel would be reprocessed, resulting in at least 96 million litres of radio-active waste pumped into the sea by Cogema, the French state firm which runs La Hague.
Greenpeace exaggerated the level of radio-activity of the waste, Electrabel said, adding in a statement that the group had taken samples before the waste was diluted in the sea.

"After having been pumped out, the waste is quickly diluted so that it becomes harmless to health and the environment," it said. It quoted an official French report saying supervision and inspection at La Hague had so far not found a single indication of possible risk for people living nearby.
"As a comparison: breathing in gases from car exhausts is toxic; breathing in the surrounding city air in which a vehicle moves is on the contrary harmless," Electrabel said.
Earlier this month the new French left-wing government ordered studies by a state agency into the levels of radio-active waste in the Channel near La Hague.

The decision followed claims by Greenpeace that it had found "stupefying" radio-activity levels, above those allowed by the European Union, in sludge on the seabed near the end of a pipe discharging waste from the plant into the sea.
